Floodwaters Recede Across Austria as Economic Activity Gradually Restarts

VIENNA – After days of record rainfall triggered widespread flooding across Austria, authorities confirmed on Monday that waters have finally receded, allowing most economic activity to resume. The disaster, which began last Thursday, swamped key transport routes, disrupted supply chains, and forced temporary shutdowns at manufacturing plants and distribution centers nationwide.

Emergency services reported that major rivers, including the Danube and the Inn, burst their banks at multiple points. The hardest-hit provinces were Upper Austria, Lower Austria, and Styria, where hundreds of residents were evacuated. National weather officials said some regions saw rainfall amounts not recorded in over 50 years.

In a statement, Interior Minister Claudia Berger praised the swift response of local and federal agencies. "Thanks to coordinated efforts, we averted greater loss of life and property," Berger said. "Our focus now is on supporting those affected and getting Austria back to work."

The Austrian Chamber of Commerce estimates the disaster halted or slowed operations at more than 900 businesses, with transport and logistics especially impacted. Freight rail lines between Linz and Vienna were submerged for almost 48 hours, and highways near Graz remained impassable until Sunday evening.

"Factories in the automotive supply, electronics, and food sectors all had to pause production or reroute goods," said Thomas Leitner, spokesperson for the chamber. "The priority now is restoring full supply chain functionality, which should be achievable within the next week."

Energy supplies remained stable throughout the event, although several hydroelectric plants operated at reduced capacity. According to the National Federation of Energy Providers, all facilities are now back online.

Shoppers in Vienna and Salzburg saw some empty supermarket shelves over the weekend, but retail association head Eva Moser reassured the public: "Distribution is returning to normal, and we expect no long-term shortages."

Unions representing logistics and warehouse workers commended employers for prioritizing safety and providing paid leave during closures. "We appreciate the cooperation shown during difficult days," said Michael Gruber, chair of the Warehouse Workers' Union.

With floodwaters receding and cleanup underway, government officials pledged continued support for affected communities and businesses as Austria moves toward full recovery.
